intro: In this college you'll learn how to talk about school in Dutch: primary school and your children, study plans, your own school days, and your goals for learning Dutch, while you practise giving reasons with 'omdat' and 'dat'.

paragraphs.heading: Welcome — school is everywhere
paragraphs.text: Welcome to theme twelve. Its title is [[Op school]], which means 'at school'. If you have children in the Netherlands, or you are taking a Dutch course yourself, school will be part of your daily life. You will talk with teachers, read letters from school, and explain your own plans. So this is very practical Dutch. Let's start with the two big words. Primary school, for children from four to twelve, is the [[basisschool]]. Secondary school, after that, is the [[middelbare school]]. A pupil is a [[leerling]], a school subject is a [[vak]], and the classroom or class is the [[klas]]. A common, friendly question between learners is [[Welk vak vind je het leukst?]], which means 'which subject do you like best?'. In this college I explain everything in English, but every Dutch word and sentence is spoken by a native Dutch voice, so you train your ear too. Please repeat each Dutch phrase out loud after me. In this theme we also practise one of the most useful pieces of grammar in the language: how to give a reason, how to say 'because' and 'that'. By the end you will be able to explain why you do things. Are you ready? [[Laten we beginnen!]]

paragraphs.heading: Your children and the basisschool
paragraphs.text: Let's talk about your children at primary school. To say your child is in primary school, you say [[Mijn kind zit op de basisschool.]] Notice the verb [[zit]], literally 'sits' — Dutch people say a child 'sits' in a school or a group. The teacher at a primary school is often a woman, and you call her the [[juf]]; a male teacher is a [[meester]] or, more generally, a [[leraar]]. Two words you will see in every school letter are [[het huiswerk]], the homework, and [[de toets]], the test. To ask about homework you say [[Heeft mijn zoon zijn huiswerk gemaakt?]], 'has my son done his homework?'. A practical cultural tip: Dutch schools regularly invite parents to a [[oudergesprek]], a short one-to-one meeting about your child. You might ask [[Wanneer is het oudergesprek?]], 'when is the parent meeting?'. Around the end of primary school, children take a national test, traditionally called the [[Cito-toets]], which helps decide the level of secondary school. Do not worry if these words feel new — you only need a handful to follow a school letter. And if a teacher uses a hard word, this sentence is gold: [[Kunt u dat nog een keer uitleggen?]], which means 'could you explain that one more time?'.

paragraphs.heading: Saying WHY: omdat and want
paragraphs.text: Now the key grammar of this theme: how to give a reason. English uses one word, 'because', but Dutch has two, and the word order is different. The easy one is [[want]]. It joins two normal sentences and changes nothing: [[Ik leer Nederlands, want ik woon hier.]] — 'I am learning Dutch, because I live here.' The verb [[woon]] stays in its normal place. The second word is [[omdat]], also 'because', but here is the surprise: after [[omdat]], the verb jumps to the very end. So the same idea becomes [[Ik leer Nederlands omdat ik hier woon.]] Hear how [[woon]] now sits at the end? Let's do a school example. With [[want]]: [[Ik ga naar school, want ik wil mijn diploma halen.]] With [[omdat]]: [[Ik ga naar school omdat ik mijn diploma wil halen.]] The verbs [[wil halen]] go right to the end. Here is your quick test: after [[omdat]] the verb moves to the end; after [[want]] it does not. Both are correct, so if the end-position confuses you, start with [[want]] and you are safe. One more, very personal: [[Ik leer Nederlands omdat ik wil inburgeren.]], 'I am learning Dutch because I want to integrate.' Try saying your own reason out loud now.

paragraphs.heading: Saying WHAT you think: dat
paragraphs.text: There is a twin of [[omdat]] that you will use constantly: the little word [[dat]], meaning 'that'. You use it after verbs of thinking, hoping, saying and knowing — [[denken]] (to think), [[hopen]] (to hope), [[zeggen]] (to say), [[weten]] (to know), and [[vinden]] (to find, to have an opinion). And just like [[omdat]], the word [[dat]] sends the verb to the end. For example: [[Ik denk dat het huiswerk moeilijk is.]], 'I think that the homework is difficult.' Hear how [[is]] goes to the end. About your child you might say [[Ik denk dat het een goede school is.]], 'I think that it is a good school.' What the teacher says: [[De juf zegt dat mijn zoon goed leert.]], 'the teacher says that my son studies well.' And your hopes: [[Ik hoop dat ik mijn diploma haal.]], 'I hope that I will get my diploma.' Sometimes two verbs land together at the end, and that is completely normal: [[Ik weet dat hij wil studeren.]], 'I know that he wants to study.' This pattern is everywhere in real conversation, so practise the formula: [[ik denk dat]], then your sentence with the verb pushed to the end. With [[omdat]] and [[dat]] together, you can now explain almost anything.

paragraphs.heading: Study plans and the Dutch school system
paragraphs.text: Let's talk about the future and the school system. To make plans, Dutch uses [[gaan]] plus a verb, or the verb [[willen]], to want. For example: [[Volgend jaar ga ik naar de middelbare school.]], 'next year I am going to secondary school.' A useful warning about two verbs: [[leren]] means to learn or study at school level, so you say [[Ik leer Nederlands]]; but [[studeren]] is only for higher education, like college or university. So a teenager says [[Mijn dochter wil later medicijnen studeren.]], 'my daughter wants to study medicine later.' Now the system itself. After the [[basisschool]], children go to one of three secondary levels. The most practical, vocational track is [[vmbo]]. The middle track, for higher professional college, is [[havo]]. And the academic track, leading to university, is [[vwo]]. You will hear these letters all the time at school, so it helps to recognise them. The goal of any track is the [[diploma]], and to 'get' or 'pass' a diploma the Dutch verb is [[halen]]: [[Mijn dochter haalt dit jaar haar diploma.]] For adults, learning happens in a [[cursus]], a course, and you finish with an [[examen]], an exam. A warm sentence to remember: [[Hij wil later aan de universiteit studeren.]], 'he wants to study at university later.'

paragraphs.heading: A real moment at the oudergesprek
paragraphs.text: Let's put it together the way it really happens, at a parent meeting. The teacher welcomes you: [[Fijn dat u er bent. Hoe gaat het thuis?]], 'nice that you are here; how are things at home?'. You answer warmly: [[Goed, dank u. Hij vindt school leuk, maar rekenen is moeilijk.]] — 'good, thank you; he likes school, but maths is difficult.' The teacher reassures you with a reason: [[Ik denk dat hij meer moet oefenen.]], 'I think that he needs to practise more.' She adds a tip: [[U kunt samen lezen, omdat hij dan meer woorden leert.]] — 'you can read together, because he then learns more words.' And you reply with hope: [[Ik hoop dat zijn cijfer beter wordt.]], 'I hope that his grade gets better.' Did you notice every reason used [[dat]] or [[omdat]] with the verb at the end? That is exactly the grammar of this theme, living in a real conversation. So this week, write three short sentences about your own life: one with [[want]], one with [[omdat]], and one with [[ik denk dat]]. Say them out loud. Remember the Dutch saying [[Al doende leert men.]] — 'you learn by doing.' [[Heel goed gedaan!]] Well done, and I will see you in the next theme!
